Ice–Vapour Chemistry

cuDisc includes a module for the adsorption and desorption of volatile molecular ices (e.g. CO, H2O) onto and off dust grains. The ice–vapour chemistry is fully coupled to the 2D dust dynamics and grain-size distribution, enabling studies of snow-line structure and volatile transport in protoplanetary discs.

The methods are described in Robinson, Owen & Booth (2026).

Physical model

The total mass of a volatile species is split between the vapour phase (density \(\rho_v\)) and the ice phase (density \(\rho_i\) per grain-size bin). The two phases are coupled by three processes:

  1. Adsorption: vapour molecules collide with grains and freeze onto the surface.

  2. Thermal desorption: ice sublimates when the surface temperature is high enough.

  3. Photodesorption: UV photons (from the stellar radiation field or cosmic rays) dislodge ice molecules from grain surfaces.

Adsorption rate

The adsorption rate onto grains of number density n with radius a is (Robinson et al. 2026, Eq. 3):

\[R_\text{ad} = \pi a^2\,v_\text{th}\,n\,\rho_v, \quad v_\text{th} = \sqrt{\frac{8 k_B T}{\pi m_\text{mol}}},\]

where mmol is the mass of a single volatile molecule.

Thermal desorption rate

Thermal desorption follows the Polanyi–Wigner law (Eq. 5):

\[R_\text{th} = 4\pi a^2\,N_s\,n\,m\,p_k\,\nu_i\, \exp\!\left(-\frac{T_\text{bind}}{T}\right),\]

where:

  • Ns = 1.5 × 1015 cm-2 is the surface site density (default).

  • m is the mass of a single ice molecule.

  • pk is the fractional surface coverage (see below).

  • νi is the characteristic oscillation frequency of the adsorbed molecule (Eq. 6):

\[\nu_i = \sqrt{\frac{2 N_s k_B T_\text{bind}}{\pi^2\,\mu\,m_H}},\]

where μ is the molecular weight and mH is the hydrogen atom mass.

  • Tbind is the binding temperature (850 K for CO, default).

Surface coverage

The fractional surface coverage interpolates between zeroth-order desorption (monolayer coverage) and first-order desorption (sub-monolayer coverage) (Eq. 7):

\[p_k = 1 - \exp\!\left(-\frac{\rho_i}{4\pi a^2 N_s n m}\right).\]

When the ice mass exceeds one monolayer, \(p_k \approx 1\) and desorption is zeroth-order (independent of coverage). Below one monolayer, \(p_k \approx \rho_i / (4\pi a^2 N_s n m)\) and desorption is first-order.

Photodesorption rate

UV photons desorb ice molecules at a rate (Eq. 8):

\[R_\text{ph} = \pi a^2\,n\,m\,p_k\,(\gamma_\text{UV} + \gamma_\text{CR})\,Y,\]

where Y = 2.7 × 10-3 is the photodesorption yield, and γUV and γCR are the UV flux and the cosmic-ray-induced UV flux, respectively. The cosmic-ray UV flux is (Eq. 9):

\[\gamma_\text{CR} = \eta_\text{CR}\,\sigma_\text{CR},\]

with ηCR = 10-17 s-1 the cosmic-ray ionisation rate. For the CO snow line, photodesorption is typically negligible.

Note

The UV photodesorption flux attenuates with column depth into the disc. The photodesorption module computes the UV optical depth along the column from the disc surface.

Implicit solver

The chemistry equations are stiff: adsorption and desorption rates can be much faster than the dynamical time step. cuDisc uses a first-order implicit iterative solver to update the ice and vapour densities at each cell (Eqs. 10–11):

\[\begin{split}\rho_v^{n+1} &= \frac{\rho_v^n + \Delta t\,R_\text{des}^{n+1}} {1 + \Delta t\,R_\text{ad}^{n+1}/\rho_v^{n+1}}, \\[4pt] \rho_i^{n+1} &= \rho_\text{tot} - \rho_v^{n+1},\end{split}\]

where \(\rho_\text{tot} = \rho_v + \rho_i\) is the total volatile mass (conserved). Iteration continues until the mean fractional change is below 10-5.

Ice in the grain-size distribution

Ice is treated as a tracer carried by the non-ice dust grains. It is distributed across grain-size bins in proportion to the ice mass fraction of each bin (Eqs. 12–15). When coagulation occurs, the ice mass fraction is transferred between bins according to the coagulation and fragmentation rates, under the assumption that ice and non-ice are uniformly mixed within each grain (rather than existing as a separate mantle on a refractory core).

Opacities with ice

When ice is present, the dust opacity must account for the mixed ice–refractory composition. cuDisc uses the Maxwell-Garnett effective medium theory to compute composite grain opacities from the ice and dust volume fractions. The optical constants of CO ice are from Gavdush et al. (2022), extended to long wavelengths with Lorentz oscillator kernels and Kramers–Kronig relations.

Vapour remapping

During the hydrostatic re-equilibration step, the gas density profile is recomputed, which changes the column density in each cell. The vapour density must be remapped consistently. This is done with a log-column interpolation scheme (Eqs. 16–18) that conserves the total vapour column density in each radial annulus.

Snow-line instability

The CO snow line can undergo a thermal instability (analogous to the Dwarf-Nova instability) when the opacity changes rapidly with temperature near the condensation point. The instability criterion derived in Robinson et al. (2026), following Pringle (1981), is

\[\frac{\mathrm{d}\log q_+}{\mathrm{d}\log T} > \frac{\mathrm{d}\log q_-}{\mathrm{d}\log T},\]

where q+ and q- are the heating and cooling rates, respectively. A simplified condition in terms of the ice column density is (Eq. 26):

\[\frac{\mathrm{d}\log\Sigma_\text{ice}}{\mathrm{d}\log T} \lesssim -4.\]

cuDisc’s 2D structure reveals that the instability is suppressed in dynamically evolving discs because vertical volatile transport prevents the limit-cycle behaviour seen in 1D models.
